Animation tools: Jitter and Rive

JuL 6, 2926 instagram) REVIEW

Original post &

TL;DR

The captured devlog introduces animation options and names Jitter before the

transcript cuts off. Official documentation separately confirms Jitter's Figma

import/export workflow and Rive's interactive animation tooling. The original
finding overstated what the captured video established and included an untested
integration recipe. Treat this as a reference for a small prototype, not a ready-to-
ship dashboard change.

What it actually is

Reviewed against'primary sources on 2026-09-27. The original caption,

transcript excerpt, and OCR above are preserved; this review did not recover the

full video.

+ Jitter is a motion-design product with Figma import and video, GIF, and Lottie
export. These capabilities are documented by Jitter, rather than inferred from
the incomplete transcript. Product documentation

+ Rive provides interactive graphics and a React runtime for rendering *.riv®
assets and controlling them from application state. React documentation

+ For new Rive integrations, the vendor recommends data binding; existing
state-machine inputs remain supported. The previous recipe mixed booleans
with triggers and asserted a runtime size without measurement. Those
instructions have been removed. Migration guide

+ The exact four-tool list and the phrase “Figma Motion/LottieFiles” are not
established by the retained transcript. No claim about that plugin's identity or
capabilities is made here.

+ Repository popularity and an open-source license are not applicable to the
deviog itself; the previous zero-star placeholder was not a measured
repository fact.

Links

* Docs: https://rive.app/docs/runtimes/react/react

Kickstarter guide

1. For an exported motion graphic, import one Figma design into Jitter and try its

timeline workflow. Check the export format and plan restrictions before adopting

it. 2. For an interactive in-app graphic, create one Rive asset in the editor. MCP is
optional; follow the official desktop setup if using it, then inspect the resulting
asset and export it for runtime use. 3. Follow the current React quickstart and
renderer guidance. Bind application state using the asset's actual view-model
property names. Do not copy the removed hard-coded “statussh” recipe into an
app without an asset implementing it. 4. Check visual states, asset-load failure,
reduced-motion behavior, and actual transfer size in a local prototype. No asset,
integration, or performance test was completed during this research review.

TL;DR

The captured devlog introduces animation options and names Jitter before the

transcript cuts off. Official documentation separately confirms Jitter's Figma

import/export workflow and Rive's interactive animation tooling. The original
finding overstated what the captured video established and included an untested
integration recipe. Treat this as a reference for a small prototype, not a ready-to-
ship dashboard change.

Kickstarter guide

1. For an exported motion graphic, import one Figma design into Jitter and try its

timeline workflow. Check the export format and plan restrictions before adopting

it. 2. For an interactive in-app graphic, create one Rive asset in the editor. MCP is
optional; follow the official desktop setup if using it, then inspect the resulting
asset and export it for runtime use. 3. Follow the current React quickstart and
renderer guidance. Bind application state using the asset's actual view-model
property names. Do not copy the removed hard-coded “statussh” recipe into an
app without an asset implementing it. 4. Check visual states, asset-load failure,
reduced-motion behavior, and actual transfer size in a local prototype. No asset,
integration, or performance test was completed during this research review.
